# Book III, Proposition 13

*A circle does not touch a circle at more points than one*

[Euclid's proof](#euclids-proof) · [In Lean](#in-lean) · [What it rests on](#what-it-rests-on) · [Mishnah](#mishnah)

> A circle does not touch a circle at more points than one, whether it touch it internally or externally.

**In Lean:** ✅ proved, as Euclid states it · Euclid's argument

<p align="center"><img src="../../figures/III/13-idea.svg" alt="Let a circle touch another from inside (red) or from outside (yellow): the straight line through the two centres (black) runs to the point of contact, so there is only one." width="420"></p>

<p align="center"><em>Let a circle touch another from inside (red) or from outside (yellow): the straight line through the two centres (black) runs to the point of contact, so there is only one.</em></p>

## Euclid's proof

<p align="center"><img src="../../figures/III/13.svg" alt="Euclid's figure for Proposition III.13, with Heath's letters" width="360"></p>

For, if possible, let the circle ABDC touch the circle EBFD, first internally, at more points than one, namely D, B.

Let the centre G of the circle ABDC, and the centre H of EBFD, be taken.

Therefore the straight line joined from G to H will fall on B, D. [III. 11]

Let it so fall, as BGHD.

Then, since the point G is the centre of the circle ABCD,

BG is equal to GD;

therefore BG is greater than HD;

therefore BH is much greater than HD.

Again, since the point H is the centre of the circle EBFD,

BH is equal to HD;

but it was also proved much greater than it: which is impossible.

Therefore a circle does not touch a circle internally at more points than one.

I say further that neither does it so touch it externally.

For, if possible, let the circle ACK touch the circle ABDC at more points than one, namely A, C,

and let AC be joined.

Then, since on the circumference of each of the circles ABDC, ACK two points A, C have been taken at random, the straight line joining the points will fall within each circle; [III. 2]

but it fell within the circle ABCD and outside ACK [III. Def. 3]: which is absurd.

Therefore a circle does not touch a circle externally at more points than one.

And it was proved that neither does it so touch it internally.

Therefore etc.

Q. E. D.

## In Lean

| | |
|---|---|
| Proof | ✅ Proved |
| Statement | The whole enunciation. Circles touching within, either inside the other, or touching without, have no common point but the point of contact. |
| Argument | Euclid's. |
| Representation | Each circle comes with a centre. Touching is read of the whole circles, so circles touching within at D that meet again at B touch within at B too; III.13 shows that they cannot meet again. |
| Reviewed | The statement and the argument read against Heath's text, for every departure from Euclid, at commit [`dcb1767`](https://github.com/jackChallis/stoicheia/commit/dcb1767) ([the record](../../review/III/13.toml)) |

From [`Elements/BookIII/Prop13.lean`](../../Elements/BookIII/Prop13.lean). Euclid's sentences are the `--` comments, and our own notes are in `/- … -/`; the lines under each sentence are the Lean that carries it out.

```lean
/-- A circle does not touch a circle at more points than one, whether it touch it internally or
externally. -/
theorem Prop13 {A B C D : Point} {ABDC EBFD ACK : Circle} (hABDC : ∃ G : Point, Centre G ABDC)
    (hEBFD : ∃ H : Point, Centre H EBFD) (hACK : ∃ O : Point, Centre O ACK) :
    ((TouchesInternally ABDC EBFD D ∨ TouchesInternally EBFD ABDC D) →
      OnCircle B ABDC → OnCircle B EBFD → B = D) ∧
    (TouchesExternally ACK ABDC A → OnCircle C ACK → OnCircle C ABDC → C = A) := by
  have within : ∀ {α β : Circle}, (∃ G, Centre G α) → (∃ H, Centre H β) →
      TouchesInternally α β D → OnCircle B α → OnCircle B β → B = D := by
    intro α β hα hβ ht hBα hBβ
    -- For, if possible, let the circle ABDC touch the circle EBFD, first internally, at more
    -- points than one, namely D, B.
    refine Classical.byContradiction fun hBD => ?_
    have htB : TouchesInternally α β B := ⟨hBα, hBβ, ht.2.2.1, ht.2.2.2⟩
    -- Let the centre G of the circle ABDC, and the centre H of EBFD, be taken.
    obtain ⟨G, hG⟩ := hα
    obtain ⟨H, hH⟩ := hβ
    -- Therefore the straight line joined from G to H will fall on B, D. [III. 11]
    have hGHD : Between G H D := Prop11 hG hH ht
    have hGHB : Between G H B := Prop11 hG hH htB
    obtain ⟨L, hG_L, hH_L⟩ := Postulate1 G H (ne_of_between hGHD)
    have hD_L : OnLine D L := on_line_of_between hGHD hG_L hH_L
    have hB_L : OnLine B L := on_line_of_between hGHB hG_L hH_L
    -- Let it so fall, as BGHD.
    have hBGD : Between B G D :=
      between_of_inside_chord hG_L hB_L hD_L (centre_inside hG) hBα ht.1 hBD
    have hBGH : Between B G H := between_cut hBGD hGHD
    -- Then, since the point G is the centre of the circle ABCD,
    -- BG is equal to GD;
    have hBG_GD : ‖B G‖ = ‖G D‖ := (len_symm B G).trans (Definition15 hG hBα ht.1)
    -- therefore BG is greater than HD;
    have hHD_BG : ‖H D‖ < ‖B G‖ := by
      rw [hBG_GD, len_symm H D, len_symm G D]
      exact len_lt_of_between (between_symm hGHD)
    -- therefore BH is much greater than HD.
    have hHD_BH : ‖H D‖ < ‖B H‖ := lt_trans hHD_BG (len_lt_of_between hBGH)
    -- Again, since the point H is the centre of the circle EBFD,
    -- BH is equal to HD;
    have hBH_HD : ‖B H‖ = ‖H D‖ := (len_symm B H).trans (Definition15 hH hBβ ht.2.1)
    -- but it was also proved much greater than it: which is impossible.
    rw [hBH_HD] at hHD_BH
    exact lt_irrefl _ hHD_BH
  -- Therefore a circle does not touch a circle internally at more points than one.
  have hinternal : (TouchesInternally ABDC EBFD D ∨ TouchesInternally EBFD ABDC D) →
      OnCircle B ABDC → OnCircle B EBFD → B = D := by
    intro h hB₁ hB₂
    /- The same argument serves with the circles' names exchanged. -/
    rcases h with h | h
    · exact within hABDC hEBFD h hB₁ hB₂
    · exact within hEBFD hABDC h hB₂ hB₁
  -- I say further that neither does it so touch it externally.
  have hexternal : TouchesExternally ACK ABDC A → OnCircle C ACK → OnCircle C ABDC →
      C = A := by
    intro h hC₁ hC₂
    -- For, if possible, let the circle ACK touch the circle ABDC at more points than one, namely
    -- A, C,
    obtain ⟨hA₁, hA₂, hout⟩ := h
    refine Classical.byContradiction fun hCA => ?_
    -- and let AC be joined.
    obtain ⟨AC, hA_AC, hC_AC⟩ := Postulate1 A C (Ne.symm hCA)
    obtain ⟨P, -, hAPC, -⟩ := exists_point_between hA_AC hC_AC (Ne.symm hCA) []
    -- Then, since on the circumference of each of the circles ABDC, ACK two points A, C have
    -- been taken at random, the straight line joining the points will fall within each
    -- circle; [III. 2]
    have hP₂ : InsideCircle P ABDC := Prop2 hABDC hA₂ hC₂ P hAPC
    have hP₁ : InsideCircle P ACK := Prop2 hACK hA₁ hC₁ P hAPC
    -- but it fell within the circle ABCD and outside ACK [III. Def. 3]: which is absurd.
    exact hout P hP₁ hP₂
  -- Therefore a circle does not touch a circle externally at more points than one.
  -- And it was proved that neither does it so touch it internally.
  -- Therefore etc.
  -- Q. E. D.
  exact ⟨hinternal, hexternal⟩
```

## Mishnah

_Our commentary: what Euclid assumes, what Lean made us say out loud, and how the result looks by modern means._

**"Whether it touch it internally or externally."** Euclid gives the two kinds of touching two different proofs. When the circles touch internally, III.11 puts both points of contact on the line of centres, and BH comes out both equal to HD and much greater than it. When they touch externally, the straight line AC falls within both circles by III.2, though circles touching externally have no point within both. Heath's figure holds both suppositions at once, and ours follows it: the oval EBFD and the thin overlap of the circles at AC are what the two arguments rule out.

**Which way is the line of centres produced?** Heath reports J. G. Camerer's objection: "it is assumed that the supposed second point of contact lies on the line of centres *produced beyond the centre of the 'outer' circle*, whereas all that is proved in III. 11 is that the line of centres *produced beyond the centre of the 'inner' circle* passes through a point of contact" (vol. 2, p. 33).

**Back through the outer centre.** Heath answers that a common point off the line of centres would bring a third with it, so that "the only hypothesis left is that the second point of contact may be *on* the line of centres but in the direction of the centre of the '*outer*' circle; and Euclid's proof disposes of this hypothesis" (vol. 2, p. 33). So Euclid, having produced the line of centres through the inner centre to D, turns back through the outer centre to B. His comparison needs the four points in the order B, G, H, D; four points that merely lie on one straight line would not give it.

**Every common point is a point of contact.** We read Definition III.3 as being about the whole circles, as III.11 does, so circles that touch internally at D and also meet at B touch internally at B too, and III.11 puts B, like D, on the line of centres. G, the centre of the outer circle, lies between B and D, two points of that circle on a straight line through it (`between_of_inside_chord`), and H then gives the order BGHD. When they touch externally, our proof takes a point between A and C, and III.2 puts it within both circles.

**The modern way.** Two circles with centres g ≠ h and radii r, s touch when |g − h| is r + s or |r − s|, as in III.11 and III.12; then at a common point x one triangle inequality among g, h, x is an equality, so x lies on the straight line gh, where one point only is r from g and s from h.
